videos.title: wayne elderton   the plays the thing (1080p)

segments.description: Introducing Wayne Elderton, one of Canada's most respected coaching educators and a national expert on game-based coaching. Wayne has created much of the Canadian Certification Curriculum and has been recognised with numerous coaching awards. In his presentation, Structured Play at York Facility, Wayne will talk about how he can implement these programs and some of the lessons that he has learned around it. Sharing his expertise in the importance of competition within your playing environment. Please welcome Wayne. Tim from Canada, and I'll be speaking on the topic of Structured Play at your club. In a presentation using Shakespeare's famous line from Hamlet, the plays the thing. I chose this because we all know that tennis coaches are very cultured. I'd like to thank Tennis Australia for giving me the opportunity to present at this year's coaches conference on the theme of the power of play. Here's a little bit about me. I have a number of certifications and I'm currently the tennis director of the North Vancouver Tennis Centre. My website is acecoach.com. Now this is all the unimportant stuff. Now let's dive in to the useful information. In this presentation, I'll be using examples from my tennis centre pictured here, which is acknowledged as a best practice operation in Canada. Just for context, NVTC is a public tennis centre with nine indoor courts. The programming runs in four seasons.

That's four quarters throughout the year, fall, winter, spring and summer. The programs are extremely successful with over 1200 session spots for adults in seven levels of programs and 200 spots for juniors in nine different levels offered each season. The programs fill for each season literally within a minute and we've crashed the city's computer registration system a number of times. And I typically have hundreds of players on waiting lists each season. But not only are we a public tennis centre, but we're a tennis Canada designated junior development centre as well. We've had numerous players become national champions in their age divisions, multiple players who went on to achieve U.S. division one scholarships and even a few who went on to become professional players. The main secret to our success, if you could call it that, is that the programming is wrapped around the priority of play. For us, it really is true that the plays the thing. I'll go into the details later, but we have dedicated play sessions connected to every program at the centre. Pretty much everything I'll cover has application to both your adult programs and your junior programs. The presentation today will be broken into two parts. Part one is the advantages of prioritizing play in all your programs. Part two is about some ideas of how to organize the play at your club. Let's start by looking at some of the advantages of basing all your clubs programming around play.

One big advantage we found in incorporating dedicated play sessions was that it increased development and skill acquisition. We found that many coaches have a misconception. They see themselves as lesson givers as opposed to play enhancers. Coaches need to understand that play drives lessons, but lessons do not necessarily drive play. In other words, if you really want to fill up your lessons, organize play. As I was exploring this concept years ago, out of curiosity I did a little experiment in our junior development program. I made two groups of eight to ten-year-old juniors. One had their training sessions three times a week, and the other also had sessions three times a week, but one of the sessions was a dedicated match play day. We tested them in a variety of tactical technical skills at the beginning and at the end of the season. The results were that at the end of the season, the group that had two training sessions and a play session were superior in all aspects of their skill development. It wasn't the results that we were expecting. It seemed rather counterintuitive since one would think having the third day as training rather than playing would produce better skill results. The superior development of the two-times practice and one-time play group were even more pronounced by the end of the whole year. One key reason was when there was play every week, both the coaches and the players saw a direct purpose for what they were doing in the training sessions

that completely impacted how they competed in matches. For the players, they could see why they were winning or losing, which motivated them to put effort into their training because they would see how practice applied in the results of their playing every week. For the coaches, they were able to see what was really landing on the players, not what they were teaching, but what was actually sticking and being used by the players. One example that we learned a lot from was one time we did a whole month on approaching the net in training, but we were seeing that they were never coming in during the weekly matches. That allowed us to quickly address what the real issues were for them to truly learn the skills. Skills are not really learned until they're performed in match play. Don't think that weekly match play just means they play and the coaches simply stand around and watch. The number one reluctance coaches have to running play sessions comes from players or parents saying things like, well, why should we pay for this when we can just play on our own? The biggest contributor to the success of these sessions is the engagement of the coach. A number of your program priorities can be evaluated and driven to higher levels by the coach's engagement in the match play sessions. Things like, if you have a system where you evaluate the skills learned, the match play is the time where the evaluation should be done to get the best picture of their real playing skills, not their practice skills.

Here's a critical point. If coaches only see the players during training, they will tend to always gravitate to isolated technical coaching to the exclusion of all else. Your job should be to develop players, not simply strokeers, who never lose a drill but have trouble winning matches. Coaches can directly help players' psychological skills and help them to emotionally navigate matches, and now this is a huge thing for many young players. Things like, they're in between point routines, their end change routines, all these can be helped. Another advantage is coaches can drive tactical themes during the match play. Things like playing lefties, playing against pushers, playing against hard hitters, etc. The coaches can help them implement tactical plans. For example, they could say something like, today in match play, we're going to pick on opponents' backhands. Here's an example of one of the tactical and psychological cards that we use for our under-12 tournament players for their match play session. You can see a number of tactics that they can pre-select, like stay in the point to outlast your opponent, which emphasizes consistency, moving them around, attacking short balls, and so on. They also pick one mental and emotional element that they'll implement, like be focused for every point, or become and ready between points, etc. Finally, there's a little section that the coach can use to have them reflect on their performance at the bottom of the card.

We have different versions of these cards for every level, starting with really simple choices they can pre-select, all the way up to eventually constructing their own match plans, which they learn how to do by having these experiences regularly. During the match play sessions, the coaches help them fill out their card before playing, and use them to debrief the players at the end. Of course, we encourage them to use these same cards for their tournaments and provide them with laminated copies to keep in their bags. The other huge advantage of dedicated play sessions is helping players learn the ins and outs of the main turning points of match play. They can learn how to break or hold serve, how to close out games and sets, how to play when up or down in the score, etc. All with the coach there to help guide them through these critical learning experiences and provide immediate feedback, instead of waiting for the trial and error learning to occur as they pick up these skills slowly through competitive experiences in the occasional tournaments. What our coaches learned is that players don't win or lose primarily because of their strokes, and coached match play provided the opportunities to address all the other issues. Without intentional dedicated play sessions, I've observed that most coaches and programs default to exclusively technical coaching and repetition drills, which don't misunderstand and misunderstand me.

They are important, but not to the exclusion of all the other critical elements to be successful as a player. Just to make myself clear, technical development is critical. And in play sessions, coaches will see the functional technical flaws that are really needed to be addressed, not possibly superficial technical mistakes that they see when players are drilling. Now let's look at part two, how to organize play at your club. As I mentioned earlier, NVTC has a setup, and the programs are a setup that they have dedicated weekly play sessions attached to every level in the system. For example, in juniors there are red play sessions, orange play sessions, green play sessions, teen play sessions, etc. For adults, it's the same, with leagues at every level, every week, at different ranges of competitiveness. In our program, we structure everything to be like many of the other sports kids participate in in Canada, which is typically two practices a week and a game. The higher level tournament players may have four or five times a week in their programs, but the principal is the same. For example, in a four-week program, they would have three practices in a game day. A five-week or a five-practice program that has five practices in a week would have four practices in a game day. The important point is to have a dedicated weekly match play time. When I consult with other clubs, that's often very ambitious, and they may have issues that make it difficult, like maybe they have groups that come only once or twice a week.

In this case, I would recommend designing one of your practices every two weeks as a play session. For example, in this approach, a program where players come twice a week on Tuesdays and Thursdays would have three sessions, the Tuesday, Thursday, and the following Tuesday. And then, that next Thursday would be the play day. The cycle would continue with every fourth session being a play day. In a twelve-week program, this would allow for six dedicated play days. A bonus is if the last day of the term is a play day, it also makes for a really good term-ending party day as well. For adults, just to not sound intimidating, our lower-level leagues are called fun plays and are typically a round robin format. For adults, these play sessions are in separate leagues at the various levels in the program. In this way, all of the other instructional drill and social programs can feed into the leagues. The coaches are encouraged to inspire all the players in their various programs to funnel into leagues. We found that once players are in leagues, the addictive nature of tennis takes over and they're hooked, which may not happen if they only take lessons. You can obviously run your leagues any way you want, but all of our adult leagues and fun plays are doubles. And doubles gives the advantage of accommodating more people and just being a better use of space. Also, more people can contribute to the financial bottom line of the program, which makes the programs more profitable.

More people means players have more opportunity to meet others and make social connections. Since all the play programs are level-based, and I'll talk about that in a moment, all our leagues and fun plays are mixed-gender leagues where teams can be made up of any combination of males and females. Our leagues and fun plays run for four weeks at a time, just so we can provide chances for more people to get in, and there's a lower barrier of time and financial commitment. One thing I'd like to highlight. In my role as head course facilitator for Tennis Canada's certification in BC, I got to see thousands of coaches over the years. And I've observed that there's often a disconnect between what the coach thinks should be happening and what they need to run successful group programs. Coaches tend to think it's all about the teaching, when in fact players are seeking meaningful experiences. Coaches must set up an environment, not just run drills, that motivates players to experience enjoyment and improvement, to get exercise, to make social connections. The coach needs to be aware of the emotional climate that they're creating in the players with their words and the activities and how they run them. Play programs like leagues and socials and junior match play are a no-brainer for providing all these advantages. Another advantage is for the coaches themselves. If they can catch the vision of being a play organizer and run leagues, these are hours that are often very profitable.

I mean, one coach can easily run a four-court league where all the players are paying a little, but it adds up to a lot. But they also are far less taxing on their bodies, especially compared to private lessons, where they have to hit for the entire hour. A coach can even structure a single group lesson session to create an environment that takes the advantages of the benefit of play and provides a more motivating experience. We've found that players take lessons not because they want to learn to follow through, even if they say they do, but what they really want is to get better at playing. To emphasize the positive experience of playing tennis, our coaches use a play-practice-play format for all the sessions, which is part of a methodology called the game-based approach. For anyone who's not familiar with that concept, it simply means everything is wrapped around the experience of play. The most simplistic definition of game-based approach is get players to experience play and help them to learn to play better. This is a different process than traditional coaching, which is to teach players to stroke and then send them off to hopefully play. We've found players are coming to play and everything needs to be wrapped around that. In each session after the warm-up, which is a modified version of what players would do in a tournament warm-up where they hit some ground strokes, serves, volleys, etc.,

they play focusing on a situation that is relevant for their level. Next, they practice implementing the tactics through functional technical instruction to solve the problems encountered in that situation. It's what I call situation training, and that's a whole other presentation. Finally, they play again, trying to implement the skills that they learn in the practice. So they play this practice, and then they play. Let's talk about level-based play. All the advantages of dedicated play sessions will be supercharged if players are in groups of compatible level. If possible, the coach needs to sort out the levels of the players, so players in sessions are at least in a similar range. Of course, the coach needs to have the authority to implement a level system. If levels are not grouped well, the sessions can still work, it's just far less effective. For adults and teens, we use a system that is used across North America, but I've added descriptors here so people have a general idea of what the levels kind of mean. Our program only goes to 4.0, since that's where the majority of recreational adult players tend to peak. For juniors, we have three levels of red, three levels of orange, three levels of green, and our tournament groups are just by age division. Our triads, as we call them, are beginners who can't serve, rally, and score. Our play-its are for players who can serve, rally, and score.

Tournament is our top level for players competing in provincial level competition, and as I mentioned before, our teens just use the adult rating system. Just one note here, you can use rating systems like the ITF's WTN, but the challenge is there's no objective way to group players until all the players in your club have had enough matched data in the system. Lower level players tend to have no matched data, but it's critical that you place them in the appropriate groups to have a good experience, which is why we prefer this particular system. At first, players self-rate by using level descriptions provided in our specific system, but over the years, we've actually created player assessments to determine which level of program they would be best suited for. By managing the levels in our programs, we experienced several benefits. Players reported a better experience in the session because of the appropriate challenge level. They improved faster because the sessions were geared to their level and what they needed to get to the next level. They were motivated to keep progressing levels, sort of like a video game, since they saw an attainable pathway that they could progress through. And probably the most important, they could practice with each other in and outside of the sessions, rather than the coach always feeding. In other words, we empowered them to become independent rather than coach dependent.

Players made closer relational connections and they played and socialized with each other outside of scheduled sessions, which is a big win in our thinking. In conclusion, to summarize everything in the presentation, I would distill it into three points. Three keys to success when you embrace the priority of play. Key number one is to understand the multiple advantages play sessions and the benefits to development for juniors and adults. Key number two is schedule dedicated weekly play sessions connected to every program and even incorporate play into your lessons by using a play practice play format. And key number three, organize around level based play to supercharge all of the programs and provide a pathway. Hopefully you can see all the benefits of wrapping everything around play in your programs. And I hope you're inspired to do it more because the play is the thing. That's a wrap. And if anyone has any questions or comments, please feel free to email me. Also, check out my website for many articles and videos mostly about game based coaching and other advanced coaching methodologies. Again, I'd like to thank Tennis Australia for this opportunity to share with you all. I'll leave you with a final Shakespeare quote. Our doubts are traitors and make us lose the good we oft might win by fearing to attempt. Remember, the play is the thing. Thank you for listening.
